subject: Biology
title: How Learning Works
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: How Learning Works.

hook.text: When you learn something new, neurons that fire together wire together—strengthening their bond.

buildup.text: This is called long-term potentiation. Repeated activation makes synapses more efficient.

discovery.text: Practice doesn't just repeat—it physically thickens neural pathways and builds myelin around them.

twist.text: Spacing study sessions over days works better than cramming. The brain needs time between sessions.

climax.text: Testing yourself strengthens recall more than rereading. Struggle is what builds the pathway.

punchline.text: Struggle is the brain's way of growing.

quiz.question: What is long-term potentiation?
options: Strengthening of synapses through repeated activation

details.summary: Learning physically changes the brain by strengthening or weakening synaptic connections between neurons. Repeated use of a neural pathway strengthens it through long-term potentiation, while unused pathways weaken through synaptic pruning.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding the neuroscience of learning explains why practice makes permanent, why spaced repetition beats cramming, and why sleep is essential for consolidating new information into lasting memory.
takeaways: Learning strengthens synaptic connections through long-term potentiation
Repetition and spaced practice build stronger neural pathways
Sleep consolidates new learning by replaying and strengthening connections

faq.question: Why does spaced repetition work better than cramming?
faq.answer: Each retrieval attempt strengthens the neural pathway more than passive review. Spacing creates slight forgetting between sessions, which forces deeper retrieval that builds stronger connections. Cramming creates shallow, temporary pathways.

faq.question: Why is sleep important for learning?
faq.answer: During sleep, the brain replays the neural patterns activated during learning, strengthening important connections and pruning irrelevant ones. Sleep deprivation impairs long-term potentiation, making it physically harder to form lasting memories.
